sweep_summary: Kutenai (kute1249) is in the catalog as fixed-dominant on a second-hand StressTyp2 quotation of Garvin 1948:37 ('penultimately stressed or finally stressed'). The only title-keyword item, McClay 2017 'Focus in Ktunaxa: word order and prosody' (UBC MA thesis), is a focus-prosody study; its abstract (DataCite, saved) reports that foci are louder and higher-pitched and says nothing about word-stress placement; the full text is behind UBC's browser-verification wall for curl and web lookups (2026-09-16 and 09-17), with no Wayback, OATD, BASE, CORE, LAC or search-engine route open today — medium priority to obtain via a browser/HarvardKey. The sweep instead fetched sources the open eScholarship scan of Morgan 1991 (the catalog's own grammar, previously cited only second-hand) and scanned its stress pages: §2.5.3 p.114 states one Penultimate Stress Assignment rule giving phrasal stress on the phrase penult and weaker word stress on each word's penult, plus rhythmical alternating stress; fn.3 p.112 confines final stress to French loans, Christian names, a very few native words and one Garvin phrase. This is a first-hand statement that confirms the fixed-dominant (penultimate) coding and refines the 'or finally stressed' clause to marginal exceptions; it should replace the StressTyp2 paraphrase as the deciding source. new_statements.quote: There is one strictly mid-level stress assignment rule, Penultimate Stress Assignment. It is responsible for full (phrasal) stress on the penultimate phonemic vowel (or on the only phonemic vowel) of every phrase. This same rule is also responsible for instances of word stress, not as strong as full phrasal stress, which occur on the penultimate phonemic vowel (or on the only phonemic vowel) of individual words in a phrase, at least where there is no conflict with full phrasal stress. There is also some evidence for a rule of Rhythmical Stress Assignment which assigns still weaker instances of stress to every second syllable of a phrase
new_statements.citation: Morgan, Lawrence R. 1991. A Description of the Kutenai Language. PhD dissertation, University of California, Berkeley, §2.5.3 'The Stress Assignment Rules', p. 114 (eScholarship open-access scan, PDF p. 138; read via tesseract scanned at 200 dpi)
new_statements.reading: Kutenai word stress is fixed penultimate (penultimate phonemic vowel of each word; monosyllables stressed on their only vowel), with a stronger penultimate PHRASAL stress that overrides clashing word stresses and a weaker alternating rhythmical stress counting leftward from the phrasal penult. Final stress is confined to exceptions: French loans, most Christian names, 'a very few' native words such as /taxta'/ 'later', and one phrase-final case quoted from Garvin 1948a p.38 (fn. 3, p. 112). This supports the catalog's fixed-dominant (penultimate) coding and narrows StressTyp2's 'penultimately stressed or finally stressed' (Garvin 1948:37) to penultimate-dominant with marginal final exceptions; Morgan states (p.114) that Garvin's facts 'are in line with the facts as reported here' once phrasal, word and rhythmical stress are distinguished. (scanned rendered 'rule' as 'tule' twice; corrected in the quote.)

sources.quote: Morgan 1991:33: "For one thing, the phrase is the domain for the assignment of the most prominent kind of stress in the language. This is full phrasal stress which is assigned to the penultimate syllable of each phrase. There is also penultimate word stress, but the penultimate syllables of words within phrases are less strongly stressed and word stresses are cancelled out by phrasal stresses when there is a conflict between the two kinds of stress assignment."
